units.title: Taxonomy
units.intro:
Taxonomy is the science of **naming and classifying** living things. In this unit you will learn **why** we classify, how **Linnaeus** arranged organisms into **seven ranks** (Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species) and gave each species a **two-part Latin name**, how to use and build a **dichotomous key**, and then walk through **all five kingdoms** of Whittaker’s system — Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia — with their groups, examples, life cycles and importance.

Work lesson by lesson: read the steps, study the tables and diagrams, answer every quick check, try the worked examples before opening the answer, then do the practice set and the 36-question unit exercise.

cards.title: 2.1 Why do we classify at all?
body: Imagine walking into a market where tomatoes, nails, soap, teff and medicine are all thrown into one big pile. You would waste hours finding anything. Shops solve this by **grouping** things that are alike. Biology has the same problem, only much bigger.

From early times people grouped plants and animals by **use** (edible, poisonous, medicinal plants), by **habit or size** (herbs, shrubs, trees) and by obvious type (insects, birds, fishes). Grouping makes living things easier to understand, remember and talk about.
**Taxonomy** is the branch of biology that deals with the **naming and classification** of organisms. A biologist who specialises in this work is a **taxonomist**.
**Step 1 — the problem:** millions of organisms are already known, new ones are discovered all the time, and there are also fossils. Nobody can learn each one separately.
**Step 2 — the solution:** taxonomists examine the **structure** of organisms carefully. Organisms that are **alike** are put in the same group; organisms that are **different** go into other groups.
**Step 3 — the result:** a system of **naming and arranging** organisms into groups, so that one name tells you a lot about the organism and its relatives.

cards.title: A short history: from Aristotle to Whittaker
body: **Aristotle** (Greek thinker, 4th century BC) made one of the first written classifications. He grouped animals by simple features such as where they live and move (land, water, air) and whether or not they have red blood. His student **Theophrastus** grouped plants as **herbs, shrubs and trees** — the same everyday grouping the textbook mentions.

**Carl Linnaeus** (1707–1778), a **Swedish botanist**, built the system we still use, more than 200 years ago. He did two great things: (1) he arranged every organism then known into a series of **increasingly general groups** (a hierarchy), based on how similar their structures are; (2) he gave every species a **two-word scientific name** (binomial nomenclature). For this he is called the **“father” of modern taxonomy**.

Later, as microscopes and chemistry improved, the number of kingdoms grew: two kingdoms (plants, animals) → three (fungi separated) → four (prokaryotes separated as Monera) → **five kingdoms**, proposed by **R. H. Whittaker in 1969**. This five-kingdom system is the one your textbook and exams use.
Your exam will most often ask: **“Who is the father of taxonomy?”** → Linnaeus. **“Who proposed the five kingdoms, and when?”** → Whittaker, 1969.

cards.title: The seven ranks (taxa) — a ladder of groups
body: In biological classification a group of any size is called a **taxon** (plural: **taxa**). Since Linnaeus, the groups are arranged as a **hierarchy**: big groups contain smaller groups, which contain even smaller groups. There are **seven main ranks**:
**Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species**
Read the ladder **downwards**: the groups get **smaller**, and the members become **more similar** to each other. Read it **upwards**: the groups get **bigger** and the members are **less similar**.
**Kingdom** — the highest (largest) rank. In this book there are five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
**Phylum** (plural: phyla) — each kingdom is divided into phyla by its main features. Example: an animal with a backbone goes into phylum **Chordata**.
**Class** — a smaller division of a phylum. Chordata contains the classes fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals.
**Order** — each class is divided into orders. Insects are split into orders mainly by their **wings**; all two-winged insects, e.g. house flies, are in order **Diptera**.
**Family** — each order contains several families. Frogs and toads are in the **same order** but **different families**.
**Genus** (plural: genera) — members are very similar. Some can interbreed but the offspring may be **infertile**, e.g. the **mule** (horse × donkey).

**Species** — the lowest (smallest) rank. Members are very similar (small differences such as flower colour) and **can interbreed to produce fertile offspring**. One genus usually has several species; the textbook gives genus *Felis* with 10 or more species — lion, tiger, leopard, cheetah, domestic cat and others.

cards.title: Hierarchy pyramid: the higher the rank, the bigger and less alike the group
King Philip Came Over For Good Soup
body: The first letter of each word gives the ranks in order from biggest to smallest. Say it three times, then write the ranks from memory.

**Tigrinya-friendly tip:** think of an address that gets smaller step by step: **ሃገር** (country) → **ዞባ** (region) → **ንኡስ ዞባ** (sub-zone) → **ዓዲ** (village) → **ስድራ** (family) → **ሰብ** (one person). The country is like the kingdom and one person is like one species: the further down you go, the smaller the group and the more alike its members. (Taxonomy has seven ranks; the address idea is the same.)

body: Read across one row to compare: human and lion share **kingdom, phylum and class** (both are mammals with backbones), then split at **order** (Primates vs Carnivora). Maize and the mushroom split from them already at **kingdom**.

The human, maize and mushroom columns follow the textbook’s table. Your textbook writes the lion as *Felis leo*; newer books use *Panthera leo*. In an exam built on this textbook, *Felis leo* is accepted.

cards.title: Worked example: how related are two organisms?
cards.problem: Use the table above. Which pair is more closely related: (a) human and lion, or (b) lion and maize? Explain using ranks.

steps.text: **Step 1 — rule:** the **lower** the rank two organisms share, the **more closely related** they are.
**Step 2 — human and lion:** same kingdom (Animalia), phylum (Chordata) and class (Mammalia). They first differ at **order**.
**Step 3 — lion and maize:** they differ already at **kingdom** (Animalia vs Plantae), so they share no rank at all in the table.
**Step 4 — conclude:** human and lion share three ranks; lion and maize share none.

cards.answer: (a) Human and lion are more closely related: they share kingdom, phylum and class, while lion and maize differ at kingdom level.

cards.title: Binomial nomenclature: one organism, one two-part name
body: **Binomial** means **two names**. Linnaeus gave every species a two-word **scientific name**, for example *Homo sapiens* (human), *Felis domestica* (domestic cat) and *Zea mays* (maize).
**Part 1 = genus name** (like a surname, shared by close relatives). **Part 2 = species name** (the particular kind inside that genus).

**Why Latin?** Common names are not universal: different people use different languages and different local names. A lion is **ኣንበሳ** in Tigrinya, *anbessa* in Amharic, *simba* in Swahili — but *Felis leo* everywhere. Latin is an old language that no longer changes, so the name stays fixed. A name from another language is **Latinised**: *Aloe massawana* is the aloe first identified near **Massawa**.
**Shortening:** after the full name has been written once, the genus may be shortened to its capital letter, e.g. *Acacia tortilis* → *A. tortilis*.

cards.title: Worked example: spot the correctly written name
cards.problem: Which is correct? A. Homo Sapiens  B. homo sapiens  C. *Homo sapiens*  D. *Homo Sapiens*

steps.text: **Step 1 — check the genus:** it must start with a capital. B fails (small h).
**Step 2 — check the species:** it must start with a small letter. A and D fail (capital S).
**Step 3 — check printing:** a printed name must be in italics. C is in italics and passes every rule.

cards.title: Worked example: classify by your own criteria (Activity 2.1)
cards.problem: Group these six organisms into two groups in two different ways: lion, maize, house fly, teff, honey bee, acacia.

steps.text: **Step 1 — choose a criterion you can observe.** Way 1: “Can it make its own food (green, photosynthesises)?”
**Step 2 — sort:** Plants: maize (*Zea mays*), teff, acacia (*Acacia tortilis*). Animals: lion (*Felis leo*), house fly (*Musca domestica*), honey bee (*Apis mellifera*).
**Step 3 — a second criterion:** “Does it have a backbone?” — Vertebrate: lion. Invertebrates: house fly, honey bee. (Plants are not grouped this way; this criterion only works inside animals.)
**Step 4 — lesson learned:** a good criterion is a feature you can **see or test**, and each organism must fall clearly into **one** group.

cards.answer: Way 1: plants (maize, teff, acacia) vs animals (lion, house fly, honey bee). Way 2 (animals only): vertebrate (lion) vs invertebrates (house fly, honey bee).

cards.title: 2.2 What is a key?
body: You find an unknown animal or plant. How do you find its name? Books that help you name organisms use a **key**: a series of questions which, when answered one after another, **lead you to the name of the specimen**.
Taxonomists use several types of keys. The most familiar one in botany and zoology is the **dichotomous key** (*dicho* = in two, *tomous* = cut: “cut in two”).

A dichotomous key is a series of **couplets**. A couplet is a **pair of statements that are mutually exclusive** — only one of the two can be true for your specimen (e.g. “wings present” / “wings absent”).
At each couplet you **decide** which statement fits. That statement either gives you the **name** (a taxon) or tells you **which couplet to go to next**.
With every step the number of possible names gets **smaller**, until only **one** possibility is left.

cards.title: How to build a dichotomous key — four steps
body: **Step a — list the features.** Write the main observable features of each organism, looking for features that make each one **different** from the others (wings? gills? hooves? diet? height?).
**Step b — pair the features.** Arrange them as **pairs of opposite statements** (aquatic with gills / terrestrial with lungs).
**Step c — read each pair.** Beside each statement write either the **name** of the organism or the **number of the next couplet**.
**Step d — continue** until **every** organism has been named.

**Golden rules:** use features you can **see or measure** (not “it looks like a cat”); never use features that change (size of a young animal, colour that fades); each couplet must split the group into **two**; with *n* organisms you need *n* − 1 couplets.

cards.title: The textbook key: goat, donkey, cow, bat, fish and hyena
head: Couplet
Statement
Leads to
body: Six animals → **five couplets** (6 − 1 = 5). Each couplet removes one animal from the list.

cards.title: Walk the key couplet by couplet

steps.text: **Couplet 1:** gills or lungs? The fish breathes with gills and lives in water — it is named here. The other five go to 2.
**Couplet 2:** wings? Only the bat has wings. Four animals remain: hyena, donkey, cow, goat.
**Couplet 3:** diet? The hyena eats flesh. Donkey, cow and goat eat plants.
**Couplet 4:** hoof? The donkey has an undivided hoof; cow and goat have divided (split) hooves.
**Couplet 5:** height? The cow is taller than 1.5 m, the goat is shorter. Every animal now has a name.

cards.title: The same key as yes/no questions
body: Every couplet can be turned into a **yes/no question**:
1. Is the animal aquatic and does it breathe with gills? **Yes** → fish. **No** (terrestrial, lungs) → go to 2.
2. Are wings present? **Yes** → bat. **No** → go to 3.
3. Is the animal flesh eating? **Yes** → hyena. **No** (plant eating) → go to 4.
4. Is the hoof undivided? **Yes** → donkey. **No** (divided) → go to 5.
5. Is it more than 1.5 m tall? **Yes** → cow. **No** → goat.
Whether written as statements or as questions, the key works the same way: **two choices at every step**.

cards.title: Worked example: use the key on an unknown animal
cards.problem: An animal lives on land, has no wings, eats grass, has split hooves and is about 0.4 m tall at the shoulder. Name it using the key.

steps.text: **Couplet 1:** lives on land → not fish → go to 2.
**Couplet 2:** no wings → not bat → go to 3.
**Couplet 3:** eats grass (herbivore) → not hyena → go to 4.
**Couplet 4:** split (divided) hooves → not donkey → go to 5.
**Couplet 5:** less than 0.5 m → goat.

cards.title: Worked example: build your own key (Activity 2.2)
cards.problem: Build a dichotomous key for snail, earthworm, spider, butterfly and ant using the features shell, wings and number of legs.

steps.text: **Step a — features:** snail: shell, no legs. Earthworm: no shell, no legs. Spider: no shell, 8 legs, no wings. Butterfly: 6 legs, wings. Ant (worker): 6 legs, no wings.
**Step b — first couplet must split the group in two:** “legs absent” (snail, earthworm) / “legs present” (spider, butterfly, ant).

**Step c — write it out:** 1a Legs absent → go to 2; 1b Legs present → go to 3. 2a Shell present → **snail**; 2b Shell absent → **earthworm**. 3a Eight legs → **spider**; 3b Six legs → go to 4. 4a Wings present → **butterfly**; 4b Wings absent → **ant**.
**Step d — check:** 5 organisms, 4 couplets (5 − 1). Every statement uses a visible feature. Every organism is named once.

cards.answer: 1 legs absent→2 / legs present→3; 2 shell→snail / no shell→earthworm; 3 eight legs→spider / six legs→4; 4 wings→butterfly / no wings→ant.

cards.title: Common mistakes with keys
body: ✗ Using a feature that is not visible on the specimen (“it is dangerous”). ✓ Use structures: legs, wings, hooves, gills.
✗ Couplets that overlap (“big” / “brown”). ✓ The two statements must be **opposites** of the same feature.
✗ Skipping a couplet because you “know” the answer. ✓ Always start at couplet 1 and follow the numbers.

cards.title: Key memory: “Two doors at every step”
body: Picture a corridor with **two doors** at every step: you open **one** door only, and behind it is either a **name** or **another pair of doors**. *Di-* = two, so dichotomous = two choices.
**Tigrinya-friendly tip:** a couplet is like the question **“እወ ወይስ ኣይፋል?”** (yes or no?) — one answer only, then move on.

cards.why: Each couplet separates off one more organism, so *n* organisms need *n* − 1 couplets: 8 − 1 = **7**.

cards.why: Couplet 4: the donkey’s hoof is **undivided**; cow and goat have **divided** hooves.

cards.title: 2.3 From two kingdoms to five
body: Taxonomy changes as technology lets biologists see **more detail inside cells and molecules**. Follow the story step by step:
**Step 1 — two kingdoms:** every organism was a **plant** or an **animal**.

**Step 2 — three kingdoms:** **fungi** were separated from plants. Fungi had been treated as plants because they have a cell wall, but the wall is chemically different: plant wall = **cellulose**, fungal wall = **chitin**. Fungi also **lack chlorophyll** and feed on dead or decaying matter.
**Step 3 — four kingdoms:** the big difference between **prokaryotes** (no true nucleus) and **eukaryotes** (true nucleus) was recognised. Prokaryotes such as bacteria became kingdom **Monera**.

**Step 4 — five kingdoms:** many simple organisms once placed with plants or animals were moved into kingdom **Protista**. The five-kingdom system was first suggested by **R. H. Whittaker in 1969** and is widely used today. It is not the only system, but it is the most accepted one at this level.

body: Learn the table **column by column**: first all the cell types (only Monera is prokaryotic), then the walls (chitin vs cellulose vs none), then nutrition (make food, absorb food, ingest food).

cards.title: Two words you must own: autotroph and heterotroph
body: An **autotroph** (*auto* = self, *troph* = feeding) produces complex organic compounds (food) from **simple inorganic molecules** such as carbon dioxide and water. Energy comes from **light** (photosynthesis) or from **chemicals** (chemosynthesis). Examples: plants, algae, cyanobacteria.

A **heterotroph** (*hetero* = other) **cannot make its own food** and depends on complex organic substances made by other organisms. Animals **ingest** (swallow) food; fungi **absorb** digested food; many bacteria and protozoa are heterotrophs too.
Tip for exam stems: “**makes** its own food” → autotroph; “**takes** food from others” → heterotroph; “**absorbs**” → fungi or saprophytic bacteria; “**ingests**” → animals or protozoa.

cards.title: Many People Find Plants Amazing
body: The five kingdoms in order from simplest to most complex: **M**onera, **P**rotista, **F**ungi, **P**lantae, **A**nimalia.
Remember the two “P”s: the first P (Protista) is **tiny and simple**, the second P (Plantae) is **big and green**.

cards.title: Key questions that place any organism in a kingdom
head: Ask in this order
If YES
If NO
rows: 1. Is the cell prokaryotic (no true nucleus)?
2. Is it mostly a single cell (or simple colony) that lives in water or damp places?
3. Does it have a chitin wall, no chlorophyll, and absorb its food?
4. Does it have cellulose walls and chlorophyll (photosynthesis)?
body: This is itself a little dichotomous key — 2.2 and 2.3 work together. (Yeast is single-celled but has a chitin wall and absorbs food, so it goes to Fungi.)

cards.title: Beyond five kingdoms: the three domains
body: Molecular studies (by **Carl Woese**) later showed that prokaryotes are of two very different kinds. Many biologists now add a rank **above** kingdom, the **domain**:
**Domain Bacteria** — ordinary bacteria and cyanobacteria (prokaryotes).
**Domain Archaea** — prokaryotes that often live in extreme places such as hot springs and very salty water.
**Domain Eukarya** — all eukaryotes: protists, fungi, plants and animals.
So in the three-domain view, the old kingdom Monera is split into two domains. For your Grade 9 exams the **five-kingdom** system of Whittaker is the main one; domains are useful background.

cards.title: Where do viruses fit? (Nowhere — and here is why)
body: Viruses are **not placed in any of the five kingdoms**. Remember from Unit 1:
**1.** A virus is **not a cell**: it is only genetic material (**DNA or RNA**) inside a **protein coat**. Kingdoms group **cellular** organisms.
**2.** A virus can **reproduce only inside a living host cell**; outside a host it shows no life activities and can even be crystallised.
**3.** It has no metabolism of its own (no respiration, no nutrition).

Because viruses show some features of living things (they reproduce and have genes) and some features of non-living things, their nature is called **ambiguous** — they lie on the border between living and non-living.

cards.title: Worked example: place an organism in its kingdom
cards.problem: An organism is multicellular, made of thread-like filaments, has no chlorophyll, has cell walls of chitin and grows on old bread. Which kingdom? Give two reasons.

steps.text: **Step 1 — cell type:** multicellular threads with walls suggest a eukaryote, so not Monera.
**Step 2 — nutrition:** no chlorophyll, grows on (absorbs food from) bread → heterotroph that absorbs food, so not Plantae.
**Step 3 — wall chemistry:** chitin, not cellulose → Fungi, not Plantae; animals have no wall at all.
**Step 4 — conclude:** kingdom Fungi (it is bread mould, *Rhizopus*).

cards.answer: Fungi — it has chitin cell walls and absorbs food without chlorophyll (saprophyte).

cards.title: 2.3.1 Monera: the simplest cells
body: All members of kingdom Monera are **prokaryotic** and **unicellular**: no true nucleus (the DNA lies free in a nucleoid region) and no membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria or chloroplasts. The kingdom contains two groups: **bacteria** and **cyanobacteria** (once called blue-green algae).

**Where are bacteria?** Everywhere life is possible: hot springs, deep ocean beds, air, water, soil, on the surfaces of objects, and inside the bodies of animals and plants. They are the **simplest and most abundant** micro-organisms.
**Shapes (useful extra):** rod-shaped = **bacilli**, spherical = **cocci**, spiral = **spirilla**.

cards.title: A. Bacteria — how they feed
body: **Nutrition** is the way an organism obtains and assimilates its food. Bacteria show **two modes**:

**1. Heterotrophic (most bacteria)** — cannot make food. **Saprophytic** bacteria feed on waste and dead organic matter (they are decomposers that recycle minerals). **Parasitic** bacteria take food from a living **host** and may cause disease.

**2. Autotrophic** — make their own food. **Photoautotrophic** bacteria use **light energy** (photosynthesis). **Chemoautotrophic** bacteria use **chemical energy** from inorganic substances such as **ammonia, hydrogen sulphide or hydrogen gas**. Nitrifying bacteria (ammonia → nitrite → nitrate) are chemoautotrophs.

cards.title: Binary fission step by step

steps.text: **Step 1 — grow:** the cell elongates (gets longer).
**Step 2 — copy:** the single chromosome (DNA) **duplicates**; the two copies move apart.
**Step 3 — split:** the cytoplasm divides into two; a new wall forms across the middle.
**Step 4 — two daughter cells** grow and divide again, every **20–30 minutes**. 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 …

body: Bacteria reproduce **asexually** by binary fission. They do not reproduce sexually, but some, like *Escherichia coli*, transfer genetic material from one cell to another by a primitive sexual process called **conjugation**.

cards.title: Worked example: how fast do bacteria multiply?
cards.problem: One bacterium divides every 30 minutes. How many bacteria are present after 3 hours, if none die?

steps.text: **Step 1 — count the divisions:** 3 hours = 180 minutes; 180 ÷ 30 = **6 divisions**.
**Step 2 — each division doubles the number:** 1 → 2 → 4 → 8 → 16 → 32 → 64.
**Step 3 — as a formula:** number = 2^(divisions) = 2⁶ = 64.

cards.answer: 64 bacteria. This is why food goes bad quickly when it is kept warm.

cards.title: B. Cyanobacteria
body: **Where:** almost every life-supporting environment — fresh water, the sea and damp soil (where they give the “earthy” smell).
**Colour:** named after their **bluish** pigment, but they may be red, pink, yellow, brown or black. The **Red Sea** turns red at times when a red-pigmented species is abundant.
**Form:** single rod-shaped or spherical cells, in **colonies** or long **filaments**. Cells are larger than other bacteria and **lack flagella**.

**Nutrition:** autotrophic with **chlorophyll**; like plants they **release oxygen** in photosynthesis. Cyanobacteria are believed to be responsible for the **first appearance of significant amounts of oxygen on Earth**. Many can also **fix atmospheric nitrogen** into nitrates or ammonia in the soil.
**Reproduction:** only asexual — **simple cell division** or **fragmentation** (a filament breaks into pieces, each grows into a new filament). No sexual reproduction.

body: **Useful:** decomposers recycle minerals; nitrogen-fixing and nitrifying bacteria make soil fertile; bacteria help make yoghurt and cheese.
**Harmful:** parasitic bacteria cause diseases in humans, animals and plants.
So in the exam “Bacteria are responsible for: oxygen in the atmosphere, recycling minerals, causing diseases” → **all of the above**.

cards.title: 2.3.2 Protista: simple eukaryotes
body: Kingdom Protista contains many **simple eukaryotes** (true nucleus). Some are **unicellular**, some **colonial**, a few **multicellular**.

Shared features: they all need a **water-based environment** (fresh water, sea or damp soil); all are **aerobic** with **mitochondria**; some have **chloroplasts** and photosynthesise; most reproduce by **binary fission** and **conjugation**; many form **cysts** (protective outer coverings) in bad conditions.
Protists are divided into **three groups by mode of nutrition**: **A. animal-like protists (protozoa)**, **B. plant-like protists (algae)** and **C. fungus-like protists (slime moulds)**.

cards.title: Protista: three groups, sorted by how they feed
A. Protozoa — animal-like protists
body: Protozoa are **heterotrophs** that **ingest** solid food (**holozoic** nutrition). Some have mouth-like parts to catch prey; others use pseudopodia to move and to engulf prey such as bacteria and other small one-celled organisms.
Protozoa are divided into **four phyla by their locomotory structure**:

**i. Sarcodina** — move by **pseudopodia** (“false feet”): cytoplasm flows into an outgrowth that grows longer. Example: *Amoeba proteus* (free-living, fresh water). *Entamoeba histolytica* is a parasite that causes **amoebic dysentery**; it spreads through **contaminated water and uncooked vegetables**.

**ii. Ciliophora** — move by **cilia**. Example: *Paramecium* (fresh water), perhaps the most complex of all single cells: covered by rows of cilia; **oral groove** leading to the mouth pore and gullet; **two nuclei** (small **micronucleus**, large **macronucleus**); **two contractile vacuoles** (front and back) that remove excess water. Reproduces asexually by binary fission and sexually by **conjugation** (exchange of micronucleus material).

**iii. Mastigophora** — move by **flagella** (whip-like). Example: *Trypanosoma*, a parasite that causes **African sleeping sickness (trypanosomiasis)**, spread by the bite of the **tsetse fly**. It harms cattle and humans: irregular fever, swelling, skin eruptions, then headache, convulsions, coma and death. Parasites are first in the **blood**, later only in the **nervous system**.

**iv. Sporozoa** — **no locomotory structure**; spore-forming and almost all **parasites**, often with two alternate hosts. Example: *Plasmodium*, the cause of **malaria**, carried by the **female *Anopheles* mosquito**.

cards.title: B. Algae — plant-like protists
body: Algae are **autotrophic**: they contain photosynthetic pigments and store carbohydrates. They may be unicellular or multicellular and are classified (into more than six phyla) by cell structure, number of flagella, reproduction and life cycle. They are grouped as **simple algae** and **complex algae**.

**i. Simple algae** — all unicellular. Phyla: **Chrysophyta** (diatoms), **Euglenophyta** (euglenoids) and **Pyrrophyta** (dinoflagellates). Floating micro-organisms in water are **plankton**: the photosynthetic part (unicellular algae) is **phytoplankton** — the **primary food source for aquatic animals**; the tiny animals are **zooplankton**.

***Euglena*** lives in muddy water of slow streams, stagnant pools and ditches polluted with animal urine and faeces. It is smaller than *Amoeba* and has a definite shape. Parts: one **flagellum** at the front, attached at the base of a flask-shaped **reservoir**; a **contractile vacuole** near the reservoir; a funnel-like mouth leading to a short **gullet**; many **chloroplasts**; **no cell wall** — shape kept by a thin flexible **pellicle**; a light-sensitive **eyespot (stigma)**. It swims **towards** light of favourable intensity but moves **away** from direct sunlight. It reproduces by **binary fission**; in bad conditions it forms a **cyst**, divides inside, and releases two daughter cells when conditions improve.
**Why is *Euglena* special?** It has chloroplasts (plant-like) but no cell wall and it moves with a flagellum (animal-like) — a good reason why a separate kingdom, Protista, was needed.

cards.title: Complex algae (seaweeds)
body: Three phyla that are wholly or partly multicellular: **Rhodophyta (red algae)**, **Phaeophyta (brown algae)** and **Chlorophyta (green algae)**. They form masses along coasts and sometimes float in the open sea.
**Green algae are the most diverse**: unicellular, filamentous, colonial and multicellular forms, in the sea, fresh water and damp soil. Examples: *Chlamydomonas*, *Spirogyra*, *Volvox*, *Ulva*.

***Chlamydomonas*** — unicellular, **two flagella** (biflagellate); one large chloroplast containing a red **eyespot (stigma)**; **two contractile vacuoles** at the front. Asexual: the nucleus divides to make **up to 16 daughter cells** inside the parent wall. Sexual: two gametes of different mating types **fuse** → zygote → thick wall and dormancy → nucleus divides to give **four** cells that grow flagella and walls.

***Spirogyra*** — **filamentous**, in slow water, ponds and ditches (dark-green hair-like masses). Each cell is independent and has a **spiral chloroplast** with **pyrenoids** (where sugar is stored as **starch**). Reproduction: (1) **fission** (cell division); (2) in bad conditions **conjugation** — the contents of one cell pass through a canal into the opposite cell, the nuclei fuse (**fertilisation**) to form a **zygote**, which gets a thick coat and becomes a **zygospore**; later it grows into a new filament.
***Volvox*** — **colonial**; each cell has **two flagella**, so the colony moves; an intercellular matrix holds the cells; darker green **daughter colonies** are often inside.
***Ulva*** (sea lettuce) — truly **multicellular** with **division of labour**; body **two cells thick**; a **holdfast** anchors it to the sea floor.

cards.title: C. Slime moulds — fungus-like protists
body: Slime moulds feed like fungi: they **absorb** nutrients. Their structure is unusual:
**Acellular slime mould:** no separate cells — one giant **multinucleate mass** of cytoplasm.

**Cellular slime mould — life cycle step by step:** (1) single free-living cells called **amoebae** feed on bacteria; (2) when food runs short they **gather** and move together as a **“slug”** (pseudoplasmodium); (3) the slug turns into a **fruiting body**; (4) the fruiting body releases many **spores**; (5) each spore produces a new amoeba — the cycle is complete.

cards.title: Worked example: name the protist from clues

steps.text: **Step 1 — movement clue:** rows of tiny hairs = **cilia** → phylum **Ciliophora**.
**Step 2 — structure clues:** oral groove + macronucleus and micronucleus → *Paramecium*.
**Step 3 — contractile vacuoles:** in fresh water, water keeps entering the cell; the contractile vacuoles collect and **pump out excess water** so the cell does not burst.

cards.answer: *Paramecium*, phylum Ciliophora (animal-like protist). Its contractile vacuoles remove excess water from the cytoplasm.

cards.title: Worked example: why classify Euglena as a protist?
cards.problem: Give two plant-like and two animal-like features of *Euglena*, and explain why it is placed in Protista.

steps.text: **Step 1 — plant-like:** it has **chloroplasts** and makes food by photosynthesis; it stores carbohydrate.
**Step 2 — animal-like:** it has **no cell wall** (only a flexible pellicle) and it **moves** with a flagellum; it has an eyespot that senses light.
**Step 3 — decide:** it is a simple, unicellular eukaryote living in water that fits neither Plantae nor Animalia → **Protista** (plant-like protist, phylum Euglenophyta).

cards.answer: Plant-like: chloroplasts, photosynthesis. Animal-like: no cell wall, moves by a flagellum. It is a simple unicellular eukaryote in water, so it is a protist.

cards.title: 2.3.3 Fungi: the absorbers and decomposers
body: Fungi are mostly **filamentous eukaryotes** with **saprophytic** nutrition. A few are **unicellular** (yeast). The filaments are **hyphae** (singular: hypha); a mass of hyphae is a **mycelium** (plural: mycelia). A mushroom is many hyphae packed tightly together.
In some fungi the hyphae are divided into separate cells by cross walls; in others the hyphae are long **multinucleate tubes** with no cross walls.

**How fungi feed:** they **secrete enzymes** onto their food, **digest it outside** the body and then **absorb** the products. They are **saprophytes** (feed on dead matter), **parasites** (feed on living hosts) or partners in a mutual association (lichens). As **decomposers** they are very important in the environment.

**Reproduction:** both asexual and sexual, by **spores**. Spores are **non-motile** and are spread by **wind or water**. Usually fungi use **asexual** spores; in bad conditions (lack of food and water) many reproduce **sexually**. Fungi are **classified by their type of sexual reproduction** into four phyla.

cards.title: The four phyla of fungi
body: **A. Zygomycota** — filamentous, cottony growth; hyphae **without cross walls**. Sexual reproduction by **conjugation** → a **zygosporangium** with zygospores, which can stay dormant until conditions are good. Example: ***Rhizopus*** (black bread mould): tubular multinucleate hyphae with creeping branches (stolons), absorbing **rhizoids** and upright **sporangiophores**; the black spore walls give the colour. On a suitable surface, mature spore-bearing mycelia form within **72 hours**.

**B. Ascomycota (sac fungi)** — asexual spores in chains called **conidia**; sexual spores in a small sac, the **ascus**, usually **eight ascospores** per ascus; many asci sit in a cup-like **ascocarp**. **Yeasts** are the simplest ascomycetes: one-celled, used for **bread, beer and wine**. In good conditions yeast multiplies by **budding** (unequal division). In bad conditions a cell divides its nucleus twice → **four ascospores** inside an ascus; these dormant spores resist drying and are sold as “active yeast”.

**C. Basidiomycota (club fungi)** — mushrooms, bracket fungi, puffballs. Spores form on a **club-shaped basidium**, each bearing **four basidiospores**. The mycelium spreads out in a circle from where the spore landed; at the edge, packed hyphae form fruiting bodies called **basidiocarps** (mushrooms). The **gills** under the cap are lined with basidia.
**D. Deuteromycota (imperfect fungi)** — fungi whose **sexual reproduction is unknown**. When a sexual stage is discovered, the fungus is moved to Ascomycota or Basidiomycota.

Lichens: a fungus and an alga working together
body: A **lichen** is an association of a **fungus** and a **green alga** living in **mutualism** — a symbiosis in which **both benefit**.
**The fungus gives:** it holds **water** to keep the alga moist, “digests” the rock surface to release **minerals** for both, and **protects** the alga.
**The alga gives:** it has **chlorophyll** and makes **organic food** for both by photosynthesis.
This is why lichens can grow on bare rocks and tree bark where neither partner could live alone.

cards.title: 2.3.4 Plants: green, multicellular, on land
body: Members of kingdom Plantae are **multicellular eukaryotes** with **cellulose** cell walls. Their cells are **specialised into tissues and organs**. They are **photosynthetic** organisms **adapted to life on land**, with pigments **chlorophyll and carotenoids**, and they **store food as starch**.

**How do plants differ from complex algae?** Algae (seaweeds) live in water and have no true tissues or organs (*Ulva* is only two cells thick); plants have tissues and organs and most are adapted to land.

cards.title: Alternation of generations — slowly, step by step
body: The plant life cycle alternates between **two generations** (two kinds of plant body):
**Step 1:** the **sporophyte** (spore-bearing plant) matures and produces **spores**.
**Step 2:** each spore grows into a **gametophyte** (gamete-producing plant).
**Step 3:** the mature gametophyte produces **gametes** (sex cells: sperm and egg).
**Step 4:** two gametes **fuse** (fertilisation) → a **zygote**.
**Step 5:** the zygote grows into a new **sporophyte** — and the cycle repeats.
**Memory hook:** *Sporophyte → spores; Gametophyte → gametes.* The name tells you what it makes.

cards.title: The four plant groups
body: Plants are classified by the **presence or absence of vessels (vascular tissue) and seeds** into four main groups: **bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms**.

**A. Bryophyta (mosses and liverworts)** — the **first land plants**, but they live in **very damp, shady places**. **No vascular tissue**, so water and food move cell to cell and the plants **stay small**. They have root-like **rhizoids** and leaf-like structures — **not** true roots or leaves. The **gametophyte is dominant**; the sporophyte depends on it for food. Spores form in a **capsule**. **Water is needed** for sperm to swim to the egg.

**B. Pteridophyta (ferns, club mosses, horsetails)** — **seedless vascular** plants with **true roots, stems and leaves**. Underground stem = **rhizome**; fern leaves = **fronds**, growing from buds on the rhizome. The **sporophyte is dominant** (much larger). The gametophyte is a tiny, independent, **heart-shaped prothallus** that does **not** depend on the sporophyte for food. Spores form in clusters (sori) on the **underside of the frond**.

**C. Gymnosperms (“naked-seed” plants)** — differ from ferns in having **seeds** and **no independent gametophyte** (it is tiny and stays inside the sporophyte). Seeds sit **on the surface of cone scales** (naked). Includes **conifers** (largest group, e.g. pine), ginkgos, cycads and gnetophytes. A pine has **staminate (male) cones**, small (less than 3 cm), and larger **ovulate (female) cones** made of scales, each scale carrying **two seeds**.

**D. Angiosperms (flowering plants)** — the gametophyte is reduced to a **few cells inside the flower**. Seeds develop in the **ovary** at the base of the flower; the ovary protects ovules better than a cone scale, and the ovary wall becomes the **fruit** that **encloses the seeds**. The **most diverse** plant group (**more than 250 000 species**). Two classes: **monocotyledons** and **dicotyledons**.

cards.title: Worked example: why are mosses small?
cards.problem: Explain why mosses grow only a few centimetres tall and only in damp places.

steps.text: **Step 1:** mosses have **no vascular tissue** (no xylem or phloem).
**Step 2:** water and food must move slowly **from cell to cell** — this only works over short distances, so the plant must stay **small**.
**Step 3:** their **sperm must swim** through water to reach the egg, and the plant body dries out easily — so they need **damp, shady** places.

cards.answer: No vascular tissue (only cell-to-cell transport) keeps them small; swimming sperm and lack of protection against drying keep them in damp places.

lessons.title: Kingdom Animalia: Body Plans and Invertebrates

cards.title: 2.3.5 Animals: what they all share
body: All animals are **multicellular** and made of **eukaryotic cells without cell walls**. Their tissues form **organs and organ systems**. They respire **aerobically**.

**Nutrition:** animals are **heterotrophs** — no chlorophyll, so they feed on plants, other animals or both. Because they must **find food**, **locomotion** is important in nearly all animals (most are motile during at least part of their life).
**Sexual reproduction (most animals):** specialised sex cells fuse at **fertilisation** to form a **zygote**, which develops into a new individual.

**Asexual reproduction (some animals):** **regeneration** — regrowth of a lost tissue or body part in an adult (e.g. a starfish arm); **parthenogenesis** — an **unfertilised** egg is activated and develops into a new organism; **budding** — an outgrowth that detaches and becomes a new individual (e.g. *Hydra*).
Animals are broadly split into **invertebrates** (no backbone) and **vertebrates** (backbone).

cards.title: Body symmetry
body: **Symmetry** describes how body parts are arranged around an axis, so that the body can be divided into similar halves.
**Asymmetrical** — no pattern; cannot be split into similar halves. The most primitive animals, e.g. **sponges**.

**Radial symmetry** — parts arranged around a **central axis**, like spokes of a wheel; can be cut through the centre in **more than one plane** to give identical halves. Usually **sessile** (fixed); reaching out in all directions helps them catch food. Examples: **cnidarians** (*Hydra*, jellyfish) and adult **echinoderms** (starfish).

**Bilateral symmetry** — only **one** plane gives two mirror-image halves (left and right). Usually active animals with a head end (**cephalisation**). Examples: flatworms, roundworms, annelids, molluscs, arthropods, vertebrates.

cards.title: A. Invertebrates — eight phyla, one by one
body: **i. Porifera (sponges)** — mostly marine, a few in fresh water. The **simplest animals**: **asymmetrical**; cells are differentiated but there are **no true tissues** and no three germ layers. Two cell layers with a jelly-like layer between, where **amoeboid cells** crawl and secrete **spicules** (mineral needles) or **spongin** (protein). **Sessile, porous filter feeders**: **collar cells (choanocytes)** beat their flagella to draw water in through the **pores** and out through the **osculum**; food is trapped by collar cells and digested **inside cells** (intracellular). Asexual by **fragmentation**; most show **sequential hermaphroditism** (one sex, then the other), which prevents self-fertilisation.

**ii. Cnidaria (coelenterates)** — jellyfish, *Hydra*, sea anemones, corals; mostly marine (*Hydra* lives in fresh water). **Radial symmetry**, **two tissue layers** with jelly between; **tentacles** with stinging **nematocysts**; a sac-like gut with **one opening** (mouth = anus). Two body forms: **polyp** (attached, mouth and tentacles **up**) and **medusa** (free-floating, mouth and tentacles **down**, an upside-down polyp). Asexual by **budding**; sexual reproduction gives a swimming larva, the **planula**, which settles and becomes a polyp.

**iii. Platyhelminthes (flatworms)** — planaria, flukes, tapeworms. **Flat**, **bilateral**, with **cephalisation** (a definite head) and organs; gut (if any) has **one opening**. **Free-living** (e.g. planaria): carnivores and scavengers in water and moist land. **Parasitic**: **flukes** (in gut, liver, lungs, bladder or blood vessels) and **tapeworms** (in the intestine; **no gut** of their own — they absorb digested food; a **scolex** for attachment and a chain of **proglottids**, each with male and female organs). Body coverings resist the host’s enzymes and immune defences. Most are **hermaphrodites** but cross-fertilise; can reproduce asexually by **transverse fission + regeneration**.

**iv. Nematoda (roundworms)** — *Ascaris*, hookworms, *Trichinella*. **Cylindrical**, **bilateral**, **unsegmented**, tapered body with a tough **cuticle** that is **moulted** during growth. **No cilia or flagella**. **Complete gut** (mouth **and** anus). Free-living in soil or parasites of animals and plants. **Separate sexes**, sexual reproduction.

**v. Mollusca** — snails, slugs, clams. **Bilateral**, soft body, distinct head, usually a **shell of calcium carbonate**. Three body parts: muscular **foot** (movement), **visceral mass** (internal organs), **mantle** (fold of tissue over the visceral mass; secretes the shell). Many have a toothed **radula** for scraping. **Open circulatory system** with a **three-chambered heart**. Mostly separate sexes.

**vi. Annelida (segmented worms)** — earthworms, leeches, polychaetes. **Bilateral**, body of ring-like **segments** separated inside by **septa**; each segment has its own circulatory, excretory, nervous, muscular and respiratory parts. **Closed circulatory system**; complete gut; most have bristles (**setae**) that anchor them during movement; most are hermaphrodites. **Earthworms** burrow in moist soil and eat decaying plant matter — they **fertilise and aerate** the soil. **Leeches** (no setae) are predators or blood-sucking parasites. The **clitellum** of earthworms and some leeches secretes a sticky substance that forms the **cocoon (egg sac)** — it is **associated with reproduction**. **Polychaetes** (e.g. *Nereis*) are marine, with tentacles and many setae.

cards.title: vii. Arthropods — the biggest phylum
body: *Arthron* = joint, *pod* = foot (leg): **jointed appendages** + a body covered by an **exoskeleton** of **chitin and protein**. These two features make arthropods the most successful animals in many environments. **Largest phylum** of the animal kingdom.
Jointed appendages work as **legs** (walking), **antennae** (sensing) and **mouthparts** (feeding). Arthropods walk, crawl, climb, hop, fly, glide or swim.
The exoskeleton protects organs, supports the body and helps movement — but it **cannot expand**, so it is **shed (moulted)** periodically for growth.

Inside: **ganglia** as a brain, a heart-like organ, complete gut and excretory system, good sense organs (antennae, eyes). Breathing by body surface, **gills**, **tracheae** or **book lungs**. **Open circulatory system**: blood pumped into the body space around the organs, then back to the heart.
Arthropods are grouped by **number of legs** (and body parts) into four groups: **arachnids, crustaceans, myriapods and insects**.

cards.title: Insects in detail
body: Insects are the **most successful invertebrates on land** thanks to: a **tracheal system** for breathing, a **cuticle** that reduces water loss, and **wings and flight** (to spread, find food, catch prey and escape).

**Body:** **head** (1 pair of antennae, eyes, mouth), **thorax** (3 segments, each with **1 pair of legs**, and usually **1 or 2 pairs of wings**; holds the main muscles), **abdomen** (stomach and reproductive organs; a sting in some). Some insects are **wingless**: ants, fleas, lice. Air enters through **spiracles** — insects have **no lungs**.
**Mouthparts:** chewing in less specialised insects (grasshopper); in others modified for **sucking, piercing and slicing** (e.g. mosquito).

**Metamorphosis** — a marked change of form during growth. **Incomplete** (grasshopper): **egg → nymph → adult** (three stages). **Complete** (butterfly, house fly): **egg → larva → pupa → adult** (four stages).

cards.title: Insect body and the two kinds of metamorphosis
viii. Echinoderms — spiny skin
body: *Echinos* = spiny, *derma* = skin. Starfish, sea urchins, sea cucumbers. **Exclusively marine** and **radially symmetrical** (parts radiate from the centre). Body forms vary — soft, cylindrical, spiny, many-armed, feathery — but all have a unique **water vascular system** used for **feeding, locomotion, respiration and sensing**. They have **no head, eyes or brain**.

**Reproduction:** asexual — a single starfish arm with a small piece of the central disc can **regenerate** the whole animal. Sexual — seasonal breeding, eggs released into the sea, **external fertilisation**, free-swimming **larvae** that develop into adults.

**Gut openings:** sponges none → cnidarians and flatworms **one** → roundworms and above **two** (mouth and anus).

cards.problem: A worm-like animal from moist soil has a body of many ring-like segments, bristles on each segment and a thick band near the front that makes a cocoon. Name it, its phylum, and the band.

steps.text: **Step 1 — worm shape options:** flat (Platyhelminthes), round unsegmented (Nematoda) or **segmented** (Annelida).
**Step 2 — segments + setae** → **Annelida**.
**Step 3 — lives in soil, makes a cocoon** → **earthworm**.
**Step 4 — the band** that secretes the sticky cocoon is the **clitellum** (used in reproduction).

cards.answer: Earthworm, phylum Annelida; the band is the clitellum, which forms the egg cocoon.

cards.title: Worked example: insect or arachnid?
cards.problem: A small animal has two body parts, eight legs and no antennae. Another has three body parts, six legs, one pair of antennae and two pairs of wings. Classify each.

steps.text: **Animal 1:** 2 body parts (cephalothorax + abdomen), **8 legs**, **no antennae** → **arachnid** (e.g. spider).
**Animal 2:** head, thorax, abdomen; **6 legs**; 1 pair of antennae; wings → **insect** (e.g. bee).
**Both** have jointed legs and an exoskeleton → phylum **Arthropoda**.

cards.answer: Animal 1 is an arachnid; animal 2 is an insect. Both are arthropods.

cards.title: B. Vertebrates — animals with a backbone
body: Vertebrates have a true, usually **bony endoskeleton**, with a **backbone** around the spinal cord and a **skull** around the brain. They belong to phylum **Chordata**. Five classes: **fishes, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals**.

**Two key words:** **poikilothermic** (“cold-blooded”) — body temperature **changes with the surroundings** (fishes, amphibians, reptiles). **Homoeothermic** (“warm-blooded”) — body temperature is kept **constant** (birds and mammals).

cards.title: i. Fishes
body: **Aquatic**, the **most diverse** vertebrate group: common fishes, sharks, skates, rays. They swim with **fins**; a **streamlined, lubricated** body makes swimming cheap in energy. Many have **scales** and all breathe by **gills**. Complete gut, **closed circulation** with a **two-chambered heart**, **poikilothermic**.
**Reproduction:** most release many eggs into water and males release sperm over them → **external fertilisation**. **Sharks** use **internal** fertilisation.

**a. Chondrichthyes (cartilaginous fishes)** — sharks and rays: skeleton of **cartilage**, true jaws, two pairs of fins, skin with **tooth-like scales**, **five pairs of gill slits** on each side of the head.

**b. Osteichthyes (bony fishes)** — skeleton of **bone**; sturgeons, eels, sea horses and most freshwater and marine fishes; overlapping scales, two-chambered heart, jaws, **covered gills (operculum)**, usually a **swim bladder** — a gas-filled bag that gives **buoyancy**.

body: Exam check: “Members of class Osteichthyes have skeletons made of **bone**” — rays and skates are cartilaginous, and all fishes here have jaws.

cards.title: ii. Amphibians
body: Frogs, toads, salamanders — **two pairs of legs**; the **first vertebrates to walk on land**. They move between water and land or spend one life stage in each (*amphi* = both, *bios* = life).

Adults mostly **carnivorous**, larvae herbivorous. A **true tongue** first appears in amphibians. They breathe through a **moist, non-scaly skin** and **lungs** (tadpoles by gills). **Three-chambered heart**; **poikilothermic**.
**Reproduction:** most frogs and toads return to **water**, lay eggs there, **external fertilisation**; eggs hatch into swimming **tadpoles** that change gradually (**metamorphosis**) into adults.

cards.title: iii. Reptiles
body: Snakes, lizards, turtles, tortoises, crocodiles, alligators. All except snakes have **two pairs of limbs** with **claws**; legs do not fully lift the body. **Dry, waterproof, scaly skin** for dry places; the outer skin layer is **shed** regularly.

Breathe by **lungs**; **poikilothermic**; heart **not completely four-chambered** — except **crocodiles** (four chambers). **Internal fertilisation** and **shelled eggs** — so reproduction does not need open water.
**Why were reptiles among the first vertebrates fully adapted to land?** Waterproof scaly skin (no drying out), lungs only, internal fertilisation, and eggs with a shell that keeps the embryo moist.

cards.title: iv. Birds
body: From the tiny humming bird to the ostrich. Four limbs, the **forelimbs modified as wings**. **Feathers are unique to birds** and do many jobs: **insulation** (birds are warm-blooded, body temperature about **40 °C**), protection from **UV rays**, incubation and **waterproofing**, **flight**, appearance and **colours** for camouflage and breeding display. Worn feathers are replaced by **moulting**.
Other features: **scales on the legs**, a **four-chambered heart**, **hollow bones** (light, for flight), **no teeth**; **homoeothermic**; they breathe faster than mammals and are warmer.

**Adaptations:** beaks match food (finch — seeds, crack; hawk — flesh, tear; swallow — insects, catch; duck — small water animals, strain). Feet match life (woodpecker — climbing; duck — swimming, webbed; pigeon — perching).

cards.title: v. Mammals
body: Mammals have **body hair**, **external ears**, and females feed young with **milk from mammary glands**. **Specialised teeth** match the diet: you can usually tell a mammal’s diet from its teeth.
**By diet:** **carnivores** (meat: lion, wolf, tiger, dog, cat), **herbivores** (plants: cow, elephant, giraffe, horse), **omnivores** (both: humans, pigs), **insectivores** (insects: anteaters).
**Homoeothermic** — so they can be active day or night and live in harsh places. Also: a **diaphragm** for efficient breathing, a **four-chambered heart**, **sweat glands**.

**Groups by birth and feeding of young:** **aplacental** mammals — **monotremes** (lay eggs; young then drink milk: **platypus**, **spiny anteater**) and **marsupials** (short-lived placenta for about 8–12 days, then the embryo grows in a **pouch**: **kangaroo**) — and **placental** mammals (a true placenta feeds the embryo through its whole development: shrews, dogs, whales, dolphins, humans).

**Warm vs cold:** only the two with **covers that trap heat** — **feathers** (birds) and **hair** (mammals) — are warm-blooded.
**Tigrinya-friendly tip:** **ዓሳ** (fish) — gills; **ዑፍ** (bird) — feathers; **ሰብ** (human) — hair and milk. Say the body covering and you know the class.

cards.title: Worked example: classify a vertebrate from clues
cards.problem: A vertebrate has dry scaly skin, breathes only with lungs, lays eggs with shells on land and its body temperature changes with the weather. Which class? Name one example from Eritrea.

steps.text: **Step 1 — skin:** dry and scaly → reptile (fishes have wet scales and gills; birds have feathers).
**Step 2 — breathing:** lungs only → not a fish or amphibian larva.
**Step 3 — eggs with shells on land, poikilothermic** → reptile, not bird (birds are homoeothermic).
**Step 4 — example:** a lizard, snake (**ተመን**) or tortoise.

cards.answer: Class Reptilia (reptiles), e.g. a lizard or a snake.

cards.title: Worked example: why is a bat a mammal and not a bird?
cards.problem: A bat flies with wings. Give three reasons it is classified as a mammal.

steps.text: **Step 1 — covering:** a bat has **hair/fur**, not feathers.
**Step 2 — young:** the female gives birth and feeds the young with **milk** from **mammary glands**.
**Step 3 — other mammal features:** **external ears** and **teeth** (birds have no teeth).
**Step 4 — lesson:** classify by **structure**, not by what the animal does (flying).

cards.answer: It has hair, feeds its young on milk from mammary glands, and has external ears and teeth.

The lowest rank; members are very similar and interbreed to produce fertile offspring.
A group of closely related species; the first part of a scientific name (plural: genera).

An organism whose cells have a true nucleus (Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia).
An organism that produces complex organic compounds from simple inorganic molecules.
An organism that cannot make its own food and depends on complex organic substances.
An organism that feeds on dead or decaying organic matter (decomposer).
Asexual division of one cell into two daughter cells (bacteria, protists).
Exchange or transfer of genetic material between two cells (E. coli, Paramecium, Spirogyra).

A “false foot”: an outflow of cytoplasm used for movement and feeding (Amoeba).
A thread of a fungus (plural: hyphae).
A mass of fungal hyphae (plural: mycelia).
A mutualistic association of a fungus and a green alga.
A symbiosis in which both partners benefit.
A small reproductive cell that grows into a new organism without fertilisation.

The small, independent, heart-shaped gametophyte of a fern.
The leaf of a fern.
The cell formed when two gametes fuse at fertilisation.
An animal with both male and female sex organs (earthworm, tapeworm).
Development of a new organism from an unfertilised egg.
Regrowth of lost tissue or a body part in an adult organism.
A marked change in form during the life cycle (insects, frogs).
Blood flows inside vessels all the time (annelids, vertebrates).
Having a body temperature that varies with the surroundings (cold-blooded).

The natural place where an organism lives.

tips.text: Learn the five-kingdom table column by column: cell type, then wall, then nutrition. Most exam questions test just one column.
For any “which kingdom/phylum/class” question, narrow down rank by rank: kingdom first, then phylum, then class.
Scientific names: capital genus, small species, italics in print, separate underlines by hand.
Keys: start at couplet 1 every time and write down your path (1 → 2 → 4 …).
Disease chains: Plasmodium → malaria → female Anopheles; Trypanosoma → sleeping sickness → tsetse fly; Entamoeba → dysentery → dirty water.
Fungi numbers: ascus 8 ascospores, basidium 4 basidiospores, yeast ascus 4.
Plants: vessels → seeds → flowers. The gametophyte shrinks at every step.
Arthropods: count legs — 6 insect, 8 arachnid; antennae — 2 pairs crustacean, none arachnid.
Vertebrate hearts: 2-3-3-4-4 (fish, amphibian, reptile, bird, mammal; crocodile has 4).

questions.q: List the four rules for writing a scientific name.
questions.answer: 1) One organism has only one scientific name. 2) It has two parts: genus then species. 3) Genus begins with a capital letter, species with a small letter. 4) Italics when printed; genus and species underlined separately when handwritten.
why: Step 1: “one” — only one scientific name per organism.
Step 2: “two” — two parts, genus first, species second.
Step 3: “capital/small” — Genus capital, species small.
Step 4: “slanted or lined” — italics in print, separate underlines by hand.
questions.tip: Remember 1-2-Capital-Italics: one name, two parts, capital first, italics.

questions.q: Why do taxonomists avoid common names and use Latin?
questions.answer: Common names differ between languages and places, so they are not universal. Latin is no longer changing, so a Latin name is fixed and the same for scientists everywhere.
why: Step 1: a common name changes with language — lion is ኣንበሳ in Tigrinya, simba in Swahili.
Step 2: one organism could have many local names, and one name could mean different organisms.
Step 3: Latin does not change and is used by scientists everywhere → one fixed name worldwide.
questions.tip: Give an example with two languages — examiners like a concrete example.

similar.q: Why is the aloe found near Massawa called *Aloe massawana*?
similar.a: The place name was Latinised to make the species name.

options.A: Members of a kingdom are more alike than members of a genus
options.B: Moving from kingdom to species, groups get smaller and members more alike

why: Step 1: species is the smallest, most specific group.
Step 2: kingdom is the biggest, least specific group.
Step 3: so going down, size decreases and similarity increases → B.
Step 4: A, C and D reverse the order.

why: Answer B: homoeothermic.

questions.q: Which statement about viruses is correct?

options.B: They are cells without a nucleus
options.C: They reproduce only inside living host cells

why: Answer C: They reproduce only inside living host cells.
Viruses are not cells and have no metabolism; they are not in any kingdom.
questions.tip: Virus = DNA/RNA + protein coat, host needed.

similar.q: What is a virus made of?
similar.a: DNA or RNA inside a protein coat.

why: Answer B: Animalia.
Sponges (Porifera) are the simplest animals → Animalia.

questions.q: An organism has cellulose cell walls, chlorophyll, vascular tissue, seeds enclosed in fruits and leaves with parallel veins. It is a
why: Answer C: monocot.
Cellulose + chlorophyll → Plantae.
Seeds in fruits → angiosperm.
Parallel veins → monocot.
questions.tip: Narrow down rank by rank: kingdom → group → class.

questions.q: Which pair of organisms are both heterotrophs that absorb their food?
why: Answer A: Yeast and mushroom.
Yeast and mushroom are fungi — absorb food.
Amoeba and Paramecium ingest food; mosses, ferns, Euglena, Volvox photosynthesise.

questions.q: During alternation of generations the ____ generation alternates with the gametophyte generation.
why: Answer: sporophyte.
The two generations are sporophyte (makes spores) and gametophyte (makes gametes).

questions.q: The two body forms of cnidarians are the polyp and the ____.
why: Answer: medusa.
Polyp = attached, mouth up; medusa = free-floating, mouth down. The planula is the larva.
questions.tip: Medusa floats like a jellyfish umbrella.

why: Answer: parthenogenesis.
An unfertilised egg develops into a new individual.

questions.q: Describe at least three ways in which bacteria obtain food.
questions.answer: Photoautotrophic (make food using light), chemoautotrophic (make food using energy from inorganic chemicals such as ammonia), saprophytic (feed on dead organic matter), parasitic (feed on a living host).
why: Step 1: split into autotrophs and heterotrophs.
Step 2: autotrophs — photo- and chemo-.
Step 3: heterotrophs — saprophytic and parasitic.
questions.tip: Two autotrophic + two heterotrophic ways = four full points.
